items.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002
items.q: Jerry Bergonzi is an example of a saxophone player who only plays for the love and the art of what he does.

ctx.x: Exactly right, or where they’re supposed to. You know Bill Holman, if anybody should be a giant in the eyes of the world and completely successful and rich to all ends it should be Bill Holman. Bill Holman is a wonderful writer, arranger, and just he’s got a mind on him that is like unique in the world. And he does fine, he does fine, there’s no problem, he does fine, but doesn’t get the acclaim or the recognition. Say Bill Holman to a bunch of kids — put ten kids in a room and say Bill Holman and you might get…

Well yeah, he should. But there’s reasons why he isn’t. Because he’s the pure art form. He is the real art form. There is no — I’m losing the word I’m thinking of — he’s not willing to compromise. It’s what it is. It’s what I do. That’s what I do and here you go. You like that? Cool. Because I’m going to keep doing that. And if you don’t like it, that’s cool too. But this is the direction I hear and that’s where I’m going. And it’s unabashed. It’s exactly what it’s supposed to be. Jerry Bergonzi is an example of…
You know just to wrap up here, I wondered if you can describe what you think of when you solo. What do you take into consideration?
